content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a user interaction-based test-time adaptation, called UITTA. When the model is not confident enough, which is decided based on the threshold automatically determined via warm up datasets, UITTA ask user to select the correct answer given top-K predictions of models. The user-feedback is then used to adapt the model to handle distribution shifts occurred at test-time. Using the number of datasets on both images and text and both constant and continual adaptation setup, they empirically show that UITTA outperforms prior test-time adaptation methods, and achieve comparable performance with online active learning (OAT), which can be regarded as an upper bound.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

**[S1]** The tackled problem is new and worth to investigate setup. 

**[S2]** The empirical validation is comprehensive and show improvement to existing approaches. 

**[S3]** Overall, the paper is easy to follow. 


**Weakness**

**[W1] Lack of discussion about technical novelty.** While I agree that user interaction-based approach is under investigated in the test-time adaptation setup, but the proposed method (eq. 3) is not tailored for test-time adaptation. In other words, the method would work with any user interaction based learning setup, e.g., standard active learning. Unfortunately, the current paper lacks discussion about the technical novelty about the proposed method, while I would say the paper still has empirical novelty. 


**[W2] Inefficiency of the proposed method.** While the empirical results support the superior performance of UITTA compared to the prior methods, UITTA still requires massive user-interaction. For example, according to Table 3, UITTA-3 requires 58% of interaction in ImageNet-C. 

In addition, I'm not sure how UITTA is efficient compared to OAL. In my understanding, the main difference between UITTA and OAL is whether the model provide options for users. In that sense, the main difference between UITTA and OAL would be UI differences, and saved human resources can be only measured via user experiments. Besides, I'm not sure whether top-k list would be better UI compared with sorting, typing, or searching. 

**[W3] Lack of in depth discussion about efficiency.** Related to the W2, the discussion about the efficacy of W2 is lacking. For example, according to Table 3, UITTA-1 saves more user resources than UITTA-3 while UITTA-3 generally perform better. Why UITTA-3 requires more user-interaction? Since UITTA-3 should give more information per one interaction, I think it is natural to expect it would save the number of interaction more than UITTA-1. 

I'm also wondering if the number of required interaction (unconfident samples) would decrease during adaptation. Since the adaptation should make the model more confident on the target distribution, the good TTA should increase the confidence as times goes on. 

**[W4] Validity of the threshold is not well discussed.** Related to the W2 and W3, the paper did not discuss whether the selected threshold is sensible or not. It would be interesting to see what happen if we increase/decrease the threshold and see tradeoff between required interaction and performance. 

**[W5] Reason behind hyperparameter is not fully explained.** In appendix, they provide detailed list of hyper parameters and its tested range, which is good, but lacks discussion on how it was selected. For example, for MRQA, they use K=1 for almost all datasets, which is wired since it contradicts with the proposals. 


**Minor comments**
- (Section 7.1) Hendrycks2020 AugMix-ResNeXt -> typo
- I'm not sure what the number presented in bottom right of Table 4. 
- Table 3 should contain standard error.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**[Clarity and Quality]**
This paper is generally well written and easy to follow. The empirical comparison is comprehensive and informative. 

**[Novelty]**
Since the paper lacks the discussion on how the proposal is technically novel and the proposal is not tailored for TTA, I evaluated the technical novelty is not high.  They provide a series of interesting experiments and therefore I evaluated empirical novelty is high. 

**[Reproducibility]**
The paper provide enough detail to reproduce the results, but the public code is preferable.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes new methodology at the intersection of online adaptation and active learning. It introduces a workable solution to adapt a model to a new domain by querying a human in the loop. Differently from standard active learning, the proposed method may require less human effort, by exposing the human to a top-K selection process, instead of asking an open question. The proposed method is tested on NLP and computer vision benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

- The proposed method, at the intersection of active learning and test-time adaptation, represents an interesting contribution for the field, given its practical utility.

- The experimental settings focuses on both NLP and computer vision tasks, supporting the applicability of the proposed approach to different learning problems.

- A method to reduce the computational burden of online test-time adaptation is proposed and empirically validated. This is a relevant contribution, since this task is well suited for practical applications

- Figures and Tables are very well designed and placed.

**Weaknesses**

- OAL is treated as an upper bound throughout the paper -- and it makes sense, since it is essentially UiTTa-N (with N=number of classes). Yet, it is not clear the real advantage of having this weaker form of asking for human help: while the reader can imagine that it will require less time for a user to provide this type of feedback, some analyses need to be carried out. For example, how much time is saved in this way, or if this allows using less experienced annotators in general.

- The proposed method is for continual/online adaptation, but performance evolution over time (update steps) is never shown or discussed. How does performance evolve, with respect to OAL? The comparison between OAL and UiTTA at the end of the sequence is an important comparison metric, but also how the performance of two methods evolve over time: does OAL require fewer update steps to reach a certain performance? If so, the time saved by using the proposed method needs to be discussed accordingly.

- Text should be more clear, I could not understand some parts (see box below).

- (Minor) While I see value in the "fast adaptation" method, I believe it would be better to investigate the first contribution more deeply, and reserve this for another paper. The two contributions are orthogonal, in my opinion it would be a significantly stronger paper with a more in-depth analysis of UiTTa vs OAL.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

Overall writing can be improved. For example, I could not understand the paragraph "UiTTa is efficient in exploiting user participation" (Section 5.2), in particular the part "as shown in the Table 3, in the setting Model Uncertainty, using around 30% to 40% user involvement can achieve comparable results to the setting of Full". From Table 3's caption, it seems that on "Full" all the test data is annotated by users, but is this case not like supervised training on the test set? It is also not clear to me what "using around 30% to 40% user involvement" means.

**Novelty**

Test-time adaptation with a human in the loop is novel and has practical utility.
content.summary_of_the_review: I see value in the proposed idea, but I think the advantages with respect to OAL are not really addressed in this paper. I look forward reading the Author response and engaging in discussions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the setting of test time adaptation to distribution shift, from the perspective of incorporating human feedback into the adaptation process. Specifically, a human is queried when the model's confidence is below a certain threshold, first for a binary yes/no and then, if needed, for the correct label out of k choices. Simulated experiments demonstrate this approach outperforming purely self-supervised methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---

- The paper proposes a simple method and evaluates it on both NLP and computer vision domains.
- The proposed method is described clearly, and generally the paper is well written and easy to follow.
- The paper studies an important problem setting that has not received as much attention in the test time adaptation literature.

Weaknesses
---

- Most notably, the paper lacks an actual user study to validate the proposed method.
- Some of the design choices of the method are not clearly motivated or ablated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality
---

My main quality concern is that the paper lacks a user study. The problem setting is intimately tied to user feedback and interaction, so without considering, and validating the method against, actual users, the paper is incomplete. Indeed, Section 5.5 shows that the proposed method is somewhat susceptible to noise in the user feedback, and I would be very curious whether this may end up being the case for, e.g., ImageNet, which is possibly difficult for users to provide good feedback for.

I also question some of the design choices. How was the two-stage feedback loop designed, and what alternatives were considered? What motivates this design over others? The random freezing past a certain layer is also not compared to, e.g., randomly freezing top layers, randomly freezing random layers, randomly choosing a layer to freeze, etc. The paper requires either more rigorous ablations of these choices or better motivation of why these choices were made over others.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the paper is reasonably well written and the experiments are sound, but there are several important improvements that can be made as laid out above. I am recommending weak reject and am happy to discuss further.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a new test-time adaptation framework: user interaction-based test-time adaptation (UiTTA). The idea is to boost the performance of test-time adaptation with user interaction information. Extensive experiments on various tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach UiTTA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is well-written and the method is easy to follow.
2. The idea of utilizing user-information is interesting. It is actually very practical in a sense as it is close to real-world setting where it is possible to obtain some sort of supervision from users at test-time.

Weaknesses:
1. How do you obtain user-feedback in your experiments? I was going over the text in the main paper but couldn’t find anything. I think it should be described in detail in section 5.1.
2. For fast adaptation using randomly freezing, it seems that the layers to freeze should depend on the type of distribution shift. For example, if the shift is low-level noise (e.g. gaussian noise), it should be much easier to adapt earlier layers. On the other hand, if the shift is high-level, for example, ImageNet-Sketch, such shift can not be easily adapted by changing earlier layers. 
3. For the methodology, you are selecting the uncertain samples by measuring the cross-entropy loss with it’s own predictions. Why use this metric to estimate uncertainty? What about other metrics, for example, entropy?

Such a setting is practical and should be relevant to industrial audience. However, i think some important details and justification for some parts of the approach are missing. Thus i am recommending weak reject.

content.title: UiTTa: Online Test-Time Adaptation by User Interaction
content.TL;DR: We explore test-time adaptation from model-user interaction.
content.abstract: We explore user interaction-based test-time adaptation (UITTA), which adapts a model to shifted test distributions with supervision signals from model-user interactions. Model adaptation in TTA can fail since models learn from the noisy pseudo-labels of the test data. UITTA achieves better adaptation from user feedback on top-K predictions within two rounds of simulated interactions. To have real-time adaptation, we further accelerate model optimization by reducing the cost of gradient backpropagation, through random dropping of backward paths. Simulation experiments on cross-lingual transfer, domain generalization, and corruption robustness show that low-cost user feedback can significantly boost TTA in performance, even competing with online active learning which however needs expensive human annotation. By accelerating pre-trained language models, we reduce 70% – 90% backpropagation cost with only a small drop in performance.
